files.model.yaml:
dsl: 1
model: web_service
title: A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts
currency: USD

description: >-
  The book's running example: a service that takes requests and keeps records, run on some
  number of ordinary hosts, sized from a stated workload and costed over five years. Requests
  arrive and data accumulates; a host has cores, memory and disk, and each of those is a chain
  that ends in a count of hosts. One of the three binds.

  It is a conditional model. Its ceilings are: the queueing margin at the busy hour; the point
  where more hosts stop helping; the working set outgrowing memory; disk filling; and a host lost
  at the busy hour. Its one measured constant is how well the stored records compress. Its one
  rate constant — CPU time per request — belongs on a rig nobody has declared, and is held as a
  labelled claim until one is.

  Vendor-neutral by construction. Nothing below names a product; every figure is a workload
  assumption, a price you would get quoted, a spec sheet, or the measured constant.

nodes:

  # -- the workload: what arrives, and what accumulates -----------------------------------------

  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3000.0, likely: 8000.0, maximum: 20000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — the busy hour, not the daily mean. Triangular, because this is an engineer's lowest,
        most likely and highest values; claiming more precision would be invention.
    range: [500, 40000]

  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how much you hold today. Nobody can
      count next quarter's busy hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they grow,
      and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The service owners estimate what the service holds today: its database and the objects users
        have uploaded, before replication, indexes or compression. It has not been counted yet, and
        counting it would turn the estimate into a fact.
    range: [1, 200]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.12, p90: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and the factor cannot be zero or less. One future
        in ten grows by less than 12% a year, and one in ten by more than 60%; outside that range
        you would be surprised. One factor for requests and for records, because users drive both.
    range: [1.0, 2.0]

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the refresh cycle this fleet is bought against"
    range: [3, 8]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n the n is a pure number, so the
      horizon has to be divided by something with the same units before it can be used as one.
      Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  # -- the host: the first numbers somebody else supplied --------------------------------------

  cores_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core/host
    value: 16
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: physical cores. A hyperthread is not a core, and a sheet that counts
        threads doubles this number without doubling the work a host does"
    range: [4, 128]

  ram_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 64
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: the modules fitted. The sheet says 64 GB and means GiB — appendix D —
        and the operating system will report less than either, which is os_reserve's job"
    range: [8, 1024]

  os_reserve:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.06, likely: 0.10, maximum: 0.18}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the share of memory the kernel, the agents and the page cache floor keep before
        the service sees any. Triangular: a floor, a usual figure, and a host with too many
        agents on it"
    range: [0.0, 0.4]

  ram_for_service:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per host
    note: >-
      Gibibytes in, decimal terabytes out — the build converts (appendix D). Declared in the
      unit the working set is counted in, so that the chain which divides one by the other
      rounds a count of hosts and not a count of hosts times nine hundred and thirty-one.
    formula: ram_per_host * (1 - os_reserve)

  # -- peak and mean --------------------------------------------------------------------------

  peak_to_mean:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: peak-to-mean ratio
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 3.5, maximum: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — the busy hour against the daily mean. Triangular, and it is a property of
        your traffic that belongs to the estate target: nothing here can measure it"
    range: [1.0, 10.0]

  mean_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: mean request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate / peak_to_mean

  # -- Little's law: how busy the fleet is -----------------------------------------------------

  service_demand:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: second * core / request
    label: CPU time per request
    note: >-
      Core-seconds of work one request costs, which is not how long a request takes. A request
      that occupies one core for twelve milliseconds has a service demand of twelve milliseconds
      whether it returns in twelve milliseconds or in twelve seconds — the difference is
      queueing, and Part II is about that difference.

      This is the model's one rate constant and it belongs on a rig (ch03). No rig is declared,
      so it is held here as an assumption whose source says what would replace it, rather than
      as a measured node with nothing behind it.
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.008, likely: 0.012, maximum: 0.020}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The lowest, likeliest and highest values are this book's own choice for the running example:
        not measured on any machine, not taken from any product. It is held as an assumption because
        no reference machine is declared in `rig/machine.yml`; `make measure-rig` on a declared
        machine replaces it with a measured one. It is triangular, with three values, because it has
        not been measured. Once it is, it becomes a normal spread around the measurement, which is a
        change of claim and not only of numbers (ch13).
    range: [0.002, 0.05]

  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: host
    value: 54
    label: hosts in the fleet
    note: >-
      **The most important node in this model, and the one a spreadsheet hides.** Sizing does not
      produce a fleet; it produces a recommendation, and then a person decides. It arrives here,
      in Part II, because a queue needs something to stand in front of — but it is decided in
      ch12, and everything downstream of it, every dollar, every watt, every ceiling, is a
      consequence of the number chosen here and not of the number the model would recommend in
      hindsight.

      Suppose the fleet were worked out afresh in each future, from that future's own inputs; it
      would sit inside every margin it was sized against, in every future. The ceilings that check
      those margins would then report no chance of crossing them, which is true by definition but
      tells you nothing. Holding the fleet as an input, one number the team decided, lets the
      ceilings ask: given what was bought, how often do the futures cross the line?
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The sizing decision, taken the usual way: the host count the model recommends (from ch10),
        worked out with every input at its point estimate. Change this number and watch the ceilings
        move; that is ch12's exercise.
    range: [4, 200]

  one_host:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: host
    value: 1
    note: "as elsewhere: a conversion has to be a host before the division means anything"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  one_core:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: core
    value: 1
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  one_request:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: request
    value: 1
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores in the fleet
    formula: hosts * cores_per_host

  busy_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores busy at the busy hour
    note: >-
      Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of cores doing work, it has nothing to do
      with how many you own, and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_demand

  utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: busy_cores / cores

  service_seconds:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: service time
    note: "service demand with the core divided out: how long one request would take alone"
    formula: service_demand * one_request / one_core

  in_flight_unqueued:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in flight, if none waited
    note: >-
      Little's law with the residence time equal to the service time: the fewest requests that can
      be in the system at this arrival rate. ch06 uses the residence time instead, which adds the
      time a request waits, and this number goes up.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_seconds

  # -- the knee ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  utilisation_cap:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation the model will admit to
    note: >-
      A modelling choice, stated rather than hidden. The waiting-time formula below divides by
      what is left of the fleet, so at a utilisation of one it divides by zero and returns
      infinity. Infinity is not a prediction. Past this point the formula has stopped describing a
      queue and started describing an arithmetic accident, so the model clamps and the ceiling
      reports that it is over.
    value: 0.98
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "where this model stops being about queues (ch06)"}

  queueing_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.3
    label: queueing margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch06 — the share of the fleet kept idle at the busy hour. The ceiling lets utilisation go up
        to one minus this margin, and no further. Declared once, it is used by the ceiling that
        checks utilisation at the busy hour (ch06), the ceiling on utilisation counting coordination
        (ch07), the chain that sizes the fleet for requests (from ch10) and the ceiling with one
        host lost (ch11), so they cannot drift apart.
    range: [0.0, 0.6]

  effective_utilisation:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: min(utilisation, utilisation_cap)

  residence_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: residence time
    note: >-
      Service time divided by the share of the fleet that is idle. That is the formula for one
      server with one queue, applied here to the whole fleet; a fleet of many cores sharing one
      stream of requests waits less than this at the same utilisation (ch06).
    formula: service_seconds / (1 - effective_utilisation)

  waiting_time:
    kind: derived
    unit: second
    label: time spent queueing
    formula: residence_time - service_seconds

  concurrency:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    label: requests in the system
    note: >-
      Little's law: the number of requests in a system is the rate they arrive at times how long
      each one stays. It assumes no pattern of arrivals and no order in which requests are served.
      It holds while the system is in a steady state: as many requests leaving as arriving. ch05 is
      about what that buys and what it does not.
    formula: peak_request_rate * residence_time

  queueing_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation at the busy hour
    of: utilisation
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      Not a capacity limit: a fleet that is busy most of the time, but short of fully busy, has not
      run out of anything; it has a queue in front of it. The margin is large because crossing it is
      paid for in waiting time by every request, not in a failure that pages the people on call
      (ch06).

  # -- what more hosts buy ----------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_count:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: hosts / one_host

  single_host_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second/host
    label: throughput of one host alone
    note: >-
      Every core of a host busy on requests and nothing else: the cores divided by the CPU time
      each request costs. The straight line of ch07 is this times the host count, and it is the
      line nobody has ever measured.
    formula: cores_per_host / service_demand

  contention:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: contention
    note: >-
      The fraction of the work that cannot be done in parallel: a lock, a single writer, a shared
      queue. It costs a fixed share of every host you add, so it flattens the scaling curve and
      never bends it downwards.
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.002, likely: 0.005, maximum: 0.015}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch07 — an assumption: it has not been fitted for this service; a fit from throughput
        measured at three fleet sizes, one a single host, would replace it. Triangular, because a
        fit gives a central value and a range rather than a shape. Its maximum is the end to
        distrust: a serial fraction can always be worse than the one you measured.
    range: [0.0, 0.05]

  crosstalk:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: crosstalk
    note: >-
      The cost of hosts having to agree with each other, which grows with the number of pairs
      rather than the number of hosts. This is the term that makes the curve turn over: past some
      count, the next host costs more in agreement than it brings in work.
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.5e-5, p90: 9.0e-5}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch07 — an assumption, not fitted for this service, though the same measurement as
        contention's would replace it: a fit from throughput at three fleet sizes, one a single
        host. It is the harder of the two to fit because it shows only in how the curve bends at
        larger fleets, and the three measured sizes usually sit at the small end. Lognormal, because
        it is wide and cannot be negative, and because a shape should not assert a hard upper limit
        on a quantity this weakly known.
    range: [0.000005, 0.0003]

  linear_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: throughput if scaling were free
    formula: hosts * single_host_throughput

  achievable_throughput:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: achievable throughput
    note: >-
      The universal scalability law. One host's throughput times the host count, divided by what
      contention and crosstalk take back. With crosstalk at zero, it approaches Amdahl's limit and
      never falls; with both at zero, it is `linear_throughput`: the straight line.
    formula: linear_throughput / (1 + contention * (host_count - 1) + crosstalk * host_count * (host_count - 1))

  scaling_efficiency:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: achievable_throughput / linear_throughput

  scaling_loss:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the fleet doing nothing useful
    of: 1 - scaling_efficiency
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.5
    because: >-
      At the margin, half the fleet's work is lost: one host in two does no useful work. The loss is
      to contention and to coordination between hosts. Nothing fails and nothing pages anyone; the
      fleet costs twice what its work is worth. A budget is the only thing this ceiling protects
      (ch07).

  peak_hosts:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: where adding hosts stops helping
    note: >-
      Where the scalability curve turns over, from the two coefficients alone: the square root of
      one-minus-contention over crosstalk. Past it, throughput falls. It is a property of the
      software, not of the budget, and no amount of money moves it.
    formula: one_host * sqrt((1 - contention) / crosstalk)

  headroom_to_peak:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: fraction of the peak already built
    formula: host_count / (peak_hosts / one_host)

  utilisation_including_coordination:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    note: >-
      The same fleet's utilisation, worked out from what it can deliver rather than from what its
      hosts could deliver alone. It is higher than `utilisation` whenever the fleet has more than
      one host, and equal at one host. The gap is the work the hosts do on each other's behalf.
    formula: peak_request_rate / achievable_throughput

  optimism:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: how much the queueing view understated it
    formula: utilisation_including_coordination / utilisation

  coordination_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, counting coordination
    of: utilisation_including_coordination
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      This ceiling keeps the queueing margin, the same margin as the ceiling labelled utilisation at
      the busy hour. It applies the margin to the capacity the fleet can deliver, counting
      coordination, rather than to the capacity its hosts would have alone. Where the two ceilings
      disagree, this one is about the system you own (ch07).

  # -- the working set: a regime change --------------------------------------------------------

  hot_fraction:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of records touched in a busy hour
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.01, likely: 0.03, maximum: 0.08}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — the working set as a share of everything held. Triangular; nobody measures
        this and everybody has an opinion, and the maximum is a service whose users all look at
        the same week's data"
    range: [0.005, 0.3]

  working_set:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: working set at horizon
    formula: stored_data * hot_fraction

  cache_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: cache margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch08 — how much of the fleet's memory is kept free of the working set, for its own daily
        swing and for the process heaps. Declared once, the ceiling on the working set checks
        against it (ch08), and from ch10 so does the chain that sizes the fleet for memory, so the
        two cannot drift apart.
    range: [0.0, 0.6]

  fleet_ram:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: memory the service can use, whole fleet
    formula: hosts * ram_for_service

  cache_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: working set against memory
    of: working_set / fleet_ram
    limit: 1
    headroom: cache_margin
    because: >-
      Past the limit, memory cannot hold the whole working set, so some reads go to disk. A
      request's time then includes waiting for those reads, and the model has no term for that wait,
      so the service time per request is no longer the number this model was built on. Nothing in a
      chain of multiplications says what it becomes (ch08), and the margin is the working set's own
      daily swing.

  # -- capacity: from what you hold to what you must buy ---------------------------------------

  record_compression:
    kind: measured
    unit: dimensionless
    label: record compression ratio
    result: records-compression

  replication_factor:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 3
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "three copies of every record, so that a host can die and take its disks with it.
        A different durability scheme substitutes its own factor here and the rest of the model
        is unchanged, which is the point of it being a node"
    range: [1, 4]

  index_overhead:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.30, maximum: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "indexes, the write-ahead log and journals as a multiplier on stored bytes.
        Triangular, and the bounds are for a service with a few indexes per table — a
        search-heavy one is off the top of this range"

  raw_per_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: raw bytes per stored byte
    formula: replication_factor * index_overhead / record_compression

  raw_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: raw disk needed at horizon
    formula: stored_data * raw_per_stored

  disk_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/host
    value: 2
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "spec sheet: one local drive. Decimal TB, not TiB — appendix D, and it is a 10%
        difference"
    range: [1, 60]

  disk_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: disk margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch11 — room to re-replicate a dead host's records onto the survivors, plus what a
        filesystem needs to keep allocating well. Declared once and used by the chain and by the
        ceiling"
    range: [0.0, 0.45]

  hosts_for_storage:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(raw_data / (disk_per_host * (1 - disk_margin)))

  installed_disk:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: hosts * disk_per_host

  disk_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: disk fill at horizon
    of: raw_data / installed_disk
    limit: 1
    headroom: disk_margin
    because: >-
      A fleet whose disks are full cannot take a dead host's records. A filesystem needs free space
      to keep allocating well, and the margin carries this as an assumption rather than a
      measurement. The margin is the same node the sizing used, so the two cannot drift apart
      (ch11). Over the limit means out of space; inside the margin means the re-replication reserve
      has been spent on data.

  # -- three chains, and the one that binds ----------------------------------------------------

  hosts_for_requests:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(busy_cores / (cores_per_host * (1 - queueing_margin)))

  hosts_for_memory:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    formula: ceil(working_set / (ram_for_service * (1 - cache_margin)))

  hosts_recommended:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts the model recommends
    note: >-
      Where a reader meets a binding constraint. Three chains produce three host counts and you buy
      the largest, which means that across this model's uncertainty the answer is sometimes set by
      CPU, sometimes by memory and sometimes by disk — and an average of the three never drops below
      all of them, but falls short of the largest whenever they are different.
    formula: max(hosts_for_requests, hosts_for_memory, hosts_for_storage)

  # -- a host dies at the busy hour ------------------------------------------------------------

  hosts_after_failure:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts after one is lost
    formula: hosts - one_host

  utilisation_after_failure:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: survivors' utilisation
    formula: busy_cores / (hosts_after_failure * cores_per_host)

  failure_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation with one host down
    of: utilisation_after_failure
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      One host down at the busy hour: its share of the requests lands on the survivors, and the
      question is whether they are still inside the queueing margin. N+1 is this ceiling with the
      margin at zero. The margin here is the queueing margin, because a fleet that has lost a host
      is still a queue (ch11).

  # -- capital ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 4500, p90: 9500}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "chassis, CPU, memory, drives and boot media, as configured. Lognormal like any
        price, and wide because a host is a configuration rather than a commodity"

  host_capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: hosts * host_price

  network_price_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 600, likely: 1100, maximum: 2200}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "switch ports, optics and cabling, amortised per host. Triangular rather than
        lognormal, although it is a price: it is a bill of materials divided by a host count
        somebody chose, so the bounds are the plausible designs rather than a market"

  network_capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: hosts * network_price_per_host

  capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: host_capex + network_capex

  # -- running it -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  host_power:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: W/host
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 220, likely: 300, maximum: 420}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "typical draw under load, per host as configured. Triangular, and one of the few
        inputs here whose bounds are physical rather than editorial: a host cannot draw less
        than it idles at, or more than its supply will give it"

  pue:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: PUE
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.35, maximum: 1.75}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch16 — facility overhead. A multiplier on IT load, and the single number a
        colocation contract is most likely to disagree with you about. Triangular: the minimum
        is a good building, the maximum is a poor one, and below one is impossible"
    range: [1.0, 2.2]

  facility_power:
    kind: derived
    unit: kW
    note: "watts in, kilowatts out — the build converts, nobody divides by a thousand by hand"
    formula: hosts * host_power * pue

  hours_per_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: hour/year
    value: 8766
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: >-
        by definition, 365.25 x 24. The quarter-day is six hours a year; leaving it out would
        understate every hourly cost by under a tenth of a per cent—the same share every year, not
        growing with the horizon. It is smaller than this model's other errors, and free to get
        right.

  annual_energy:
    kind: derived
    unit: kWh/year
    formula: facility_power * hours_per_year

  electricity_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/kWh
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 0.085, p90: 0.21}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "all-in delivered rate including transmission. Lognormal: it cannot go negative and
        its history is multiplicative"
    range: [0.04, 0.45]

  annual_energy_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: annual_energy * electricity_price

  licence_per_core:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/core/year
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 40, p90: 160}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the platform software's per-core licence, as quoted. Lognormal: a price, and a
        wide one, because it is the line item most often negotiated. It is what makes the core
        count a cost as well as a capacity (ch15)"

  licence_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host/year
    value: 0
    label: licence per host
    note: >-
      A declared zero, not an absent line. For a quote that licenses the platform software per core,
      as the design the plan was built on does, there is no per-host charge. For a quote that
      licenses per host, as ch22's challenger does, the per-host figure goes here and zero goes in
      `licence_per_core`. A comparison needs the same lines on both sides: a line one quote does not
      have is a cost that quote does not pay, and the way to leave it out is to put it in at zero
      (ch22).
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        The design the plan was built on is licensed per core, with no per-host charge. When a
        design licenses per host, that figure goes here and zero in `licence_per_core`, allowing the
        two to be compared like for like.
    range: [0, 12000]

  annual_licences:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    note: >-
      Both licence lines, whichever of them a quote uses. One of the two is a declared zero on
      any given quote, and keeping both is what lets two quotes with different licence models
      be subtracted from each other (ch22).
    formula: cores * licence_per_core + hosts * licence_per_host

  support_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: 1/year
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.07, likely: 0.11, maximum: 0.18}}
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "annual support as a fraction of capital cost. Triangular because it is
        negotiated inside a band the market sets rather than drawn from one: the spread is
        what different buyers get, not what varies from year to year"

  annual_support:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: capex * support_rate

  staff_fte:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: engineers, full-time equivalent
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.5, likely: 1.0, maximum: 2.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        Engineers this fleet occupies, full-time equivalent. Triangular, and the shape cannot
        express what happens: people are not divisible, so the real spread moves in whole people.

  fully_loaded_salary:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/year
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 115000, p90: 195000}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "salary, employer costs, tooling and overhead. Lognormal because pay is
        right-skewed and cannot go negative; the p90 is a senior engineer in an expensive city"

  annual_staff_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: staff_fte * fully_loaded_salary

  annual_opex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    formula: annual_energy_cost + annual_licences + annual_support + annual_staff_cost

  lifecycle_opex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    formula: annual_opex * horizon

  migration_cost:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: USD
    value: 0
    label: one-off cost of moving to this design
    note: >-
      A declared zero for the design the plan was built on, because it already runs on that
      platform. A design that would replace it carries the cost of the move here: the months of
      running both, the data copied twice, the people doing that instead of their jobs. The buyer
      pays for the move, not either vendor: a challenger's quote has no line for it, and a plan
      built on the incumbent has nothing to put in it. That is why it is a node with a source rather
      than a footnote (ch22).
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The design the plan was built on runs on that platform already, so there is nothing to
        migrate. A challenger's scenario overrides this with the team's own estimate of the move,
        marked as an assumption.
    range: [0, 1000000]

  tco:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: total cost of ownership
    note: >-
      Capital, running cost over the horizon, and whatever it costs to get there. The last term
      is zero for the design the plan was built on and is the first thing to look for in a
      comparison that was not (ch22). One purchase: the horizon is the refresh cycle, so the
      refresh that ends it belongs to the next plan's capital, not this total (ch15).
    formula: capex + lifecycle_opex + migration_cost

  # -- unit economics: two denominators for one fleet ------------------------------------------

  seconds_per_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: second/year
    value: 31557600
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: "by definition, 365.25 x 86,400"

  average_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: mean request rate over the horizon
    note: >-
      It is the mean of the day-one and horizon mean rates—a straight line between the two ends of
      the horizon. The rate compounds, so the curve bends upward and the line lies above it,
      overstating requests served and making cost per million requests come out low, more so the
      faster growth is. It is kept because the error runs one way, so you know which way to correct
      it. The exact average becomes zero divided by zero when there is no growth, a case
      `annual_growth`'s range includes, so a formula cannot branch around it. Stated rather than
      hidden, because a unit cost is only as defensible as its denominator (ch17).
    formula: (peak_request_rate_t0 / peak_to_mean + mean_request_rate) / 2

  requests_over_horizon:
    kind: derived
    unit: request
    formula: average_request_rate * seconds_per_year * horizon

  cost_per_million_requests:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/megarequest
    label: cost per million requests
    note: >-
      The formula divides dollars by requests and the node is declared per million of them, so
      the build supplies the factor. Two honest unit costs come out of this fleet, and they tell
      different stories about the same money (ch17).
    formula: tco / requests_over_horizon

  average_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    note: >-
      It is the mean of the day-one and horizon holdings: a straight line between the two ends of
      the horizon. The holding compounds, so the curve bends upward and the line lies above it,
      overstating what is held on average. Cost per stored terabyte-month comes out low, more so the
      faster growth is; ch17 shows by how much. It follows the same convention as the mean request
      rate, for the same reason: the exact average becomes zero divided by zero when there is no
      growth.
    formula: (stored_data_t0 + stored_data) / 2

  cost_per_stored_tb_month:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/TB/month
    label: cost per stored TB per month
    note: >-
      In each future, it divides that future's total by that future's straight-line holding, so it
      is neither a ratio of two middle values nor a denominator from ch17's problems. It divides by
      a horizon in years and is declared in months. Identical dimensions, a factor of twelve apart,
      so a check comparing only dimensions would publish a figure twelve times too large and pass.
      The build converts, and Appendix D lists the conversion.
    formula: tco / average_stored / horizon

outputs:
  # The sizing and the price, first: what a reader of ch12 and ch18 wants.
  - hosts_recommended
  - hosts
  - tco
  - cost_per_million_requests
  - cost_per_stored_tb_month
  - capex
  - annual_opex
  - annual_energy
  # The ceilings, and what each one is about.
  - queueing_headroom
  - failure_headroom
  - cache_fill
  - disk_fill
  - scaling_loss
  - coordination_headroom
  # Part II's own figures. Terminal in the finished model, and outputs because a quantity the
  # book quotes has to be one -- a node that feeds nothing and is reported nowhere is a leftover.
  - utilisation
  - residence_time
  - waiting_time
  - concurrency
  - in_flight_unqueued
  - optimism
  - headroom_to_peak

correlations:
  - a: peak_request_rate_t0
    b: service_demand
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      The unhappy one. A busier service is usually a slower one per request — caches miss more,
      locks are held longer, the garbage collector runs while somebody is waiting. Treating the
      two as independent understates the tail of every figure in this model, and it understates
      it exactly when the fleet is busiest.

  - a: host_price
    b: network_price_per_host
    rho: 0.5
    because: >-
      Both are quoted by the same supply chain in the same quarter. A year when hosts are scarce
      is usually a year when optics are, and treating them as independent narrows the interval
      on capital cost by pretending one can save you from the other.

files.model.yaml:
dsl: 1
model: observability
title: An observability platform — metrics, logs and traces
currency: USD

description: >-
  The book's second model, and the counterweight to the web service. Three chains of
  multiplications, metrics, logs and traces, share their roots, so they move together whether or not
  the model says so. Label cardinality is a product of uncertain counts, and it drives the active
  series count and the query path. The control knobs are sampling and retention, not money. Three
  tiers—ingest, retention store and query path—carry four ceilings between them, and no single
  number summarises them.

  It has a gap in it: two measured constants have no measurement yet. Spans per request is an
  `estate` observation: only a running system with instrumented applications can give it, not a body
  of data or a machine. The traces chain needs it. Collector throughput per core is a `rig`
  measurement, taken on the reference machine, and the measured ingest ceiling needs it. The figures
  that depend on them are shown as not yet measured rather than filled in with a plausible number,
  because a plausible number would print the same as a measured one.

nodes:

  # -- shared roots ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Everything below flows from these five. That is what makes the three chains correlated by
  # construction: they are not three models, they are one estate seen three ways.

  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: host
    value: 1200
    note: >-
      No band: an estate is a thing you can count, and this one has been counted. What it does
      next is growth_factor's business, not this node's.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the estate's host count as stated by its operators"}
    range: [50, 3000]

  request_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 8000.0, likely: 25000.0, maximum: 90000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — the busy hour across the estate, not the daily mean. Triangular, because a dashboard
        gives a lowest, a typical and a highest value and nothing more. The maximum is the busiest
        hour on record, not the busiest there will be
    range: [2000, 200000]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.15, p90: 1.70}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — telemetry grows faster than the traffic it describes, because teams add
        instrumentation as well as load. Lognormal like any growth rate — it compounds and
        cannot go negative — and wider than the web service's for the same reason its
        median is higher"

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 3
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the planning horizon for this platform"}
    range: [1, 5]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    note: "as in the web service model: an exponent has to be a pure number"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  growth_factor:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  # -- label cardinality: the combinatorial node ------------------------------------------------

  label_values_endpoint:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 6.0, maximum: 20.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        distinct routes appearing as a label value. Triangular because the routes can be counted, so
        the range is known; the maximum is the routes that exist today, and a new service adds to it

  label_values_status:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 3.0, maximum: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        distinct status classes kept as a label. Triangular, and its bounds are firm unlike those of
        any other input in the model, because a request cannot carry a status the code does not emit

  label_values_accidental_extra:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: extra accidental label values
    note: >-
      The label nobody planned: a pod name under a rolling deploy, a customer id added during an
      incident, a version string. Counted from the second value, because a label with one value
      multiplies the series count by one, so this input can only add series, never take any away.
      Lognormal and wide, because the failure mode is multiplicative: whatever the label is, it
      multiplies every series that carries it, and the band has to span from usually a little to
      occasionally catastrophic.
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 0.42, p90: 5.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch08 — the cardinality explosion, as a band rather than as a warning. Lognormal because this
        one has no ceiling: a label carrying a user id multiplies the series count by a number
        nobody chose, and a triangular would assert a maximum that does not exist. Counted from the
        second value, so the factor it feeds is never below one.

  label_values_accidental:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: accidental label values
    note: >-
      One plus the extra values: the number of values the accidental label takes. That is the factor
      it multiplies the series count by, and it is never below one.
    formula: 1 + label_values_accidental_extra

  label_cardinality:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: label cardinality
    note: >-
      It is the product of three uncertain counts: the endpoint label's values, the status label's
      values, and the accidental label's values. Its lognormal-ish shape comes from the multiplying,
      not from anyone choosing it. The accidental label leads the tornado for the active series
      count, metrics ingest and query path utilisation, and the product's band is wider than any one
      count's but much narrower than the counts' bands multiplied together, because the model draws
      them independently, so a high one usually meets middling or low ones. Appendix F sets each
      factor's range beside the product's.
    formula: label_values_endpoint * label_values_status * label_values_accidental

  # -- chain one: metrics ------------------------------------------------------------------------

  base_metrics_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/host
    value: 60
    label: metric names per host
    note: >-
      No band: scrape one host and list them. The uncertainty in this chain is what the labels
      multiply that list by, and label_cardinality carries it.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "distinct metric names exposed per host, before labels"}
    range: [10, 400]

  active_series:
    kind: derived
    unit: series
    formula: hosts * base_metrics_per_host * label_cardinality * growth_factor

  scrape_interval:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: second
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob: doubling it halves the metrics
      chain and loses resolution that cannot be recovered afterwards"}
    range: [10, 120]

  one_sample_per_series:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: sample/series
    value: 1
    note: "one scrape takes one sample from one series. A rate is a count over a duration, and the
      count needs a unit before the division means anything"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  sample_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: sample/series/second
    formula: one_sample_per_series / scrape_interval

  metrics_sample_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/sample
    label: bytes per sample, compressed
    result: metrics-sample-bytes

  metrics_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: metrics ingest
    formula: active_series * sample_rate * metrics_sample_bytes

  metrics_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 400
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob"}
    range: [15, 800]

  metrics_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: metrics_ingest * metrics_retention

  # -- chain two: logs ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  lines_per_request:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: line/request
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3.0, likely: 9.0, maximum: 30.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "application log lines emitted per request served. Triangular, from reading a
        sample of the logs — and the maximum is the part to distrust, because a debug flag
        left on in production is outside it"

  log_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 1.0
    label: fraction of log lines kept
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob: drop and aggregation rules"}
    range: [0.05, 1.0]

  log_line_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: line/second
    formula: request_rate * lines_per_request * log_keep_rate * growth_factor

  logs_line_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/line
    label: bytes per log line, compressed
    result: logs-line-bytes

  logs_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: logs ingest
    formula: log_line_rate * logs_line_bytes

  logs_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob"}
    range: [3, 365]

  logs_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: logs_ingest * logs_retention

  # -- chain three: traces, and the constant nobody has measured ------------------------------------

  spans_per_request:
    kind: measured
    unit: span/request
    label: spans per request
    note: >-
      Not measurable from anything in this repository. It is a property of one instrumented
      application at one version, so it belongs to the `estate` target — an observation somebody
      takes of a system they run, disclosed rather than verified (ch03). Until somebody takes it,
      every figure below is absent rather than estimated.
    result: traces-spans-per-request

  trace_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.05
    label: trace sampling rate
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob, and the one with the widest
      range: head sampling at 1% and at 100% are two different platforms"}
    range: [0.001, 1.0]

  span_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: span/second
    formula: request_rate * spans_per_request * trace_keep_rate * growth_factor

  traces_span_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/span
    label: bytes per span, compressed
    result: traces-span-bytes

  traces_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: traces ingest
    formula: span_rate * traces_span_bytes

  traces_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 14
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob"}
    range: [1, 90]

  traces_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: traces_ingest * traces_retention

  # -- output one: the ingest pipeline ---------------------------------------------------------------

  known_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: ingest, metrics and logs only
    note: >-
      Metrics plus logs, and deliberately not the total. The traces chain is missing because spans
      per request is not measured yet, so it is too low and serves as a lower bound. ch20 is about
      this shape of error: correct arithmetic over an incomplete structure looks identical to a
      number that is right.
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest

  total_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest + traces_ingest

  collector_cores:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core
    value: 16
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the ingest tier"}
    range: [8, 512]

  collector_throughput_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: MB/s/core
    value: 6
    note: >-
      No band, and giving a quote one would be inventing a range nobody quoted. A vendor states a
      single number; the spread belongs to the measurement, and collector_throughput_measured
      below carries it with a standard error.
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "throughput per core as documented by the collector. Unverified here, and marked as
        a claim in every figure it appears in"

  collector_throughput_measured:
    kind: measured
    unit: MB/s/core
    label: collector throughput per core, measured
    note: >-
      The same quantity as the node above, taken rather than quoted. It needs the reference
      machine (`rig`) and nobody has run it, so the ceiling built on it is absent while the
      ceiling built on the vendor's claim is not. This node sits beside
      `collector_throughput_quoted` in ch03, so the pipeline capacity each gives can be compared.
    result: collector-throughput-per-core

  quoted_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_quoted

  measured_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_measured

  quoted_pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, quoted
    of: known_ingest / quoted_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      A queueing ceiling, not a capacity one (ch06), so the margin is large: a pipeline at 80% of
      quoted throughput has a queue in front of it, and a queue in front of an ingest pipeline is
      dropped telemetry exactly when something is going wrong. Understated twice over — the
      numerator excludes traces and the denominator is a vendor's claim.

  pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, measured
    of: total_ingest / measured_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      The honest version of the row above, and it cannot be computed. Both halves are missing a
      measurement, which is the correct output of this model today.

  # -- output two: the retention store -----------------------------------------------------------

  usable_tb_per_node:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/node
    value: 40
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "usable capacity per storage node after replication"}
    range: [20, 400]

  store_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 12
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the retention tier"}
    range: [5, 400]

  installed_usable:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: store_nodes * usable_tb_per_node

  known_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: stored, metrics and logs only
    formula: metrics_stored + logs_stored

  store_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: retention store fill
    of: known_stored / installed_usable
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.3
    because: >-
      Capacity, with a rebuild reserve (ch11) — and again a lower bound, because the traces chain
      is not in the numerator. A verdict of `ok` here means "ok, ignoring traces", which is a
      different claim and one the reader should be made to notice.

  # -- output three: the query path -----------------------------------------------------------------

  queries_per_second:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: query/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 12.0, maximum: 60.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "dashboards, alert rules and people, at the busy hour. Triangular because two of
        those three are countable and the third is not"

  series_per_query_base:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/query
    label: series per query, before labels
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 40.0, likely: 300.0, maximum: 2000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "how many distinct metric-name-and-host combinations one dashboard panel or alert
        rule covers, before any label expansion. Triangular, and wide: dashboards differ from
        each other more than anything else in this model does"

  series_per_query:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/query
    note: >-
      The same cardinality node that drives the metrics ingest chain drives this one too, by a
      different route: a label that multiplies the series a scrape produces also multiplies the
      series a query has to walk past to ignore. That is why one accidental label breaks two
      ceilings at once, and why turning down scrape interval and retention — which fix the first
      — does nothing at all for the second.
    formula: series_per_query_base * label_cardinality

  query_series_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: queries_per_second * series_per_query

  query_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 24
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the query tier"}
    range: [2, 120]

  query_scan_rate_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/second/node
    value: 90000
    note: >-
      No band, for the same reason as the collector's quoted throughput: a quote is one number,
      and widening it here would put a range in the vendor's mouth. Nobody has measured this one,
      so nothing in this model disputes it yet.
    provenance: {kind: vendor_claim, source: "series scanned per second per query node, quoted"}

  query_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: query_nodes * query_scan_rate_quoted

  query_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: query path utilisation
    of: query_series_rate / query_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      Queueing again, and the tier where a breach is most visible: a dashboard that times out
      during an incident is the failure people remember. Cardinality feeds this and the ingest
      ceiling by different routes, so a single accidental label breaks both at once.

  # -- a small cost tail ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  storage_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/TB/month
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 9.0, p90: 24.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        all-in cost of a usable TB-month on this tier. Lognormal because it is a price, and a price
        cannot go below zero. It was copied by hand from another model's unit economics, as a range,
        rather than passed across with that model's own spread. That seam between two models is
        ch18's subject

  known_storage_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/month
    label: retention cost, metrics and logs only
    formula: known_stored * storage_price

outputs:
  - metrics_ingest
  - logs_ingest
  - traces_ingest
  - traces_stored
  - known_ingest
  - known_stored
  - active_series
  - label_cardinality
  - known_storage_cost
  - store_fill
  - quoted_pipeline_utilisation
  - query_utilisation
  - pipeline_utilisation

correlations:
  - a: annual_growth
    b: label_values_accidental_extra
    rho: 0.5
    because: >-
      A platform that is growing is a platform that is being changed, and labels arrive with
      changes. Treating the two as independent makes the metrics interval narrower than the
      estate warrants — ch14 measures by how much.

  - a: request_rate
    b: lines_per_request
    rho: 0.3
    because: >-
      Weak and positive: busier services tend to be the chattier ones. Small enough to be worth
      including as an example of a correlation that barely matters, which is a useful thing for a
      reader to see beside one that does.

  - a: request_rate
    b: queries_per_second
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      A busier platform is one more people are watching. Moderate rather than strong: most query
      load comes from alert rules and dashboards on timers, which do not care how busy anything
      is — right up until an incident, when they all fire at once and nobody is looking at the
      model.
