files.model.yaml:
dsl: 1
model: mixed_pool
title: Two generations in one pool
currency: USD

description: >-
  The web service's fleet as ch10 sizes it, with one change: some of last generation's hosts are
  still in service, doing the same job as the new ones. The question stops being how many hosts
  and becomes how many new hosts, given the old ones. The demand is ch10's, at its point
  estimates, so this model has no ranges: its lessons are in its structure. How requests are
  spread decides whether the two generations' capacity adds. Data is placed by capacity in both
  cases; only the routing of requests changes.

nodes:
  # -- the demand: the web service's own chain, node for node (ch02 - ch09) -------------------------
  # Copied with its shapes, sources and correlation, so busy cores, working set and data on disk
  # carry the running example's ranges rather than a second, made-up copy of them.

  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3000.0, likely: 8000.0, maximum: 20000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — the busy hour, not the daily mean. Triangular, because this is an engineer's lowest,
        most likely and highest values; claiming more precision would be invention.
    range: [500, 40000]

  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how much you hold today. Nobody can
      count next quarter's busy hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they grow,
      and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The service owners estimate what the service holds today: its database and the objects users
        have uploaded, before replication, indexes or compression. It has not been counted yet, and
        counting it would turn the estimate into a fact.
    range: [1, 200]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.12, p90: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and the factor cannot be zero or less. One future
        in ten grows by less than 12% a year, and one in ten by more than 60%; outside that range
        you would be surprised. One factor for requests and for records, because users drive both.
    range: [1.0, 2.0]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n the n is a pure number, so the
      horizon has to be divided by something with the same units before it can be used as one.
      Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  service_demand:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: second * core / request
    label: CPU time per request
    note: >-
      Core-seconds of work one request costs, which is not how long a request takes. A request
      that occupies one core for twelve milliseconds has a service demand of twelve milliseconds
      whether it returns in twelve milliseconds or in twelve seconds — the difference is
      queueing, and Part II is about that difference.

      This is the model's one rate constant and it belongs on a rig (ch03). No rig is declared,
      so it is held here as an assumption whose source says what would replace it, rather than
      as a measured node with nothing behind it.
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.008, likely: 0.012, maximum: 0.020}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The lowest, likeliest and highest values are this book's own choice for the running example:
        not measured on any machine, not taken from any product. It is held as an assumption because
        no reference machine is declared in `rig/machine.yml`; `make measure-rig` on a declared
        machine replaces it with a measured one. It is triangular, with three values, because it has
        not been measured. Once it is, it becomes a normal spread around the measurement, which is a
        change of claim and not only of numbers (ch13).
    range: [0.002, 0.05]

  busy_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores busy at the busy hour
    note: >-
      Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of cores doing work, it has nothing to do
      with how many you own, and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.
    formula: peak_request_rate * service_demand

  hot_fraction:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of records touched in a busy hour
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.01, likely: 0.03, maximum: 0.08}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — the working set as a share of everything held. Triangular; nobody measures
        this and everybody has an opinion, and the maximum is a service whose users all look at
        the same week's data"
    range: [0.005, 0.3]

  working_set:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: working set at horizon
    formula: stored_data * hot_fraction

  record_compression:
    kind: measured
    unit: dimensionless
    label: record compression ratio
    result: records-compression

  replication_factor:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 3
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "three copies of every record, so that a host can die and take its disks with it.
        A different durability scheme substitutes its own factor here and the rest of the model
        is unchanged, which is the point of it being a node"
    range: [1, 4]

  index_overhead:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.30, maximum: 1.60}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "indexes, the write-ahead log and journals as a multiplier on stored bytes.
        Triangular, and the bounds are for a service with a few indexes per table — a
        search-heavy one is off the top of this range"

  raw_per_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: raw bytes per stored byte
    formula: replication_factor * index_overhead / record_compression

  raw_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: raw disk needed at horizon
    formula: stored_data * raw_per_stored





  os_reserve:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.06, likely: 0.10, maximum: 0.18}}
    label: memory the operating system keeps
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Triangular, as in the web service model's os_reserve at its point estimate (ch10). The same share on
        both generations"

  # -- the two generations ----------------------------------------------------------------------

  cores_per_new_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core/host
    value: 16
    label: cores per new host
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, physical cores"
    range: [4, 128]

  ram_per_new_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 64
    label: memory per new host
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, the modules fitted"
    range: [8, 1024]

  disk_per_new_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/host
    value: 2
    label: disk per new host
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, one local drive"
    range: [1, 60]

  cores_per_old_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: core/host
    value: 8
    label: cores per old host
    note: >-
      One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: last generation's hosts have half the cores of this
        generation's. Fixed, because the hosts are already bought"
    range: [2, 64]

  ram_per_old_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 128
    label: memory per old host
    note: >-
      One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: last generation's hosts were bought memory-heavy, with
        twice this generation's memory and half its cores"
    range: [8, 1024]

  disk_per_old_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB/host
    value: 2
    label: disk per old host
    note: >-
      One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: the same drive as the new hosts"
    range: [1, 60]

  old_hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: host
    value: 30
    label: old hosts still in service at the horizon
    note: >-
      Not how many old hosts there are today: how many are still running at the horizon. Old
      hosts retire on their own schedule, and the check has to hold at the worst point, after
      they leave and before demand stops growing. The old_retired scenario is that point.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: thirty of last generation's hosts are kept in service
        to the horizon. A decision, because keeping them is a choice"
    range: [0, 120]

  new_hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: host
    value: 35
    label: new hosts to buy
    note: >-
      The purchase, decided the usual way: the count the model recommends when requests are
      routed by capacity, at the point estimates. Held as an input, as the web service holds
      its fleet, so the ceilings can ask how the pool as bought fares.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the sizing decision: new_hosts_weighted at the point estimates (ch10, ch12)"
    range: [2, 120]

  one_host:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: host
    value: 1
    label: one host
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition

  # -- margins, as the web service declares them ------------------------------------------------

  queueing_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.3
    label: queueing margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the web service model's queueing margin (ch06, ch11): how far under the knee the
        fleet runs at the busy hour"
    range: [0.0, 0.6]

  cache_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: cache margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the web service model's cache margin (ch08, ch11): room for the working set to grow
        before it spills out of memory"
    range: [0.0, 0.5]

  disk_margin:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.25
    label: disk margin
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the web service model's disk margin (ch11): room to re-replicate a dead host's
        records onto the survivors"
    range: [0.0, 0.45]

  # -- memory each generation gives the service -------------------------------------------------

  ram_for_service_new:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per new host
    formula: ram_per_new_host * (1 - os_reserve)

  ram_for_service_old:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per old host
    formula: ram_per_old_host * (1 - os_reserve)

  # -- what the old hosts already give, per chain ------------------------------------------------

  old_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores the old hosts give
    formula: old_hosts * cores_per_old_host

  old_ram:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: memory the old hosts give the service
    formula: old_hosts * ram_for_service_old

  old_disk:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: disk the old hosts give
    formula: old_hosts * disk_per_old_host

  # -- routed by capacity: each generation adds its share ---------------------------------------
  # What each chain still needs once the old hosts have given theirs: max(need, old) - old is
  # the need left over, or nothing, in the chain's own unit.

  new_for_requests:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts the requests need, routed by capacity
    formula: ceil((max(busy_cores / (1 - queueing_margin), old_cores) - old_cores) / cores_per_new_host)

  new_for_memory:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts the working set needs
    formula: ceil((max(working_set / (1 - cache_margin), old_ram) - old_ram) / ram_for_service_new)

  new_for_storage:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts the data needs
    formula: ceil((max(raw_data / (1 - disk_margin), old_disk) - old_disk) / disk_per_new_host)

  new_hosts_weighted:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts to buy, requests routed by capacity
    formula: max(new_for_requests, new_for_memory, new_for_storage)

  # -- routed equally: every host takes the same share ------------------------------------------
  # Each host is sent the same share of the requests, so the smallest host reaches its margin
  # first, and the pool can take no more than every host times the smallest host's cores.

  smallest_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core/host
    label: cores on the smallest host
    formula: min(cores_per_old_host, cores_per_new_host)

  new_for_requests_equal:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts the requests need, routed equally
    formula: max(ceil(busy_cores / (smallest_cores * (1 - queueing_margin))), old_hosts) - old_hosts

  new_hosts_equal:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: new hosts to buy, requests routed equally
    formula: max(new_for_requests_equal, new_for_memory, new_for_storage)

  # -- the pool as bought ------------------------------------------------------------------------

  all_hosts:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts in the pool
    formula: old_hosts + new_hosts

  pool_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core
    label: cores in the pool
    formula: old_cores + new_hosts * cores_per_new_host

  utilisation_weighted:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation, requests routed by capacity
    formula: busy_cores / pool_cores

  utilisation_smallest_equal:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: the smallest host's utilisation, requests routed equally
    formula: busy_cores / (all_hosts * smallest_cores)

  queueing_headroom_weighted:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation at the busy hour, routed by capacity
    of: utilisation_weighted
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      The web service's queueing ceiling (ch06), for a pool whose router sends each host requests
      in proportion to its cores. Then every host is equally busy and the pool's cores add up.

  queueing_headroom_equal:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: the smallest host's utilisation, routed equally
    of: utilisation_smallest_equal
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      The same ceiling for a router that sends every host the same share. The old hosts have
      fewer cores, so they are the busiest, and they reach the knee first while the new hosts
      have cores to spare. The pool bought for capacity-weighted routing is checked here too.

  # -- a shard lives on one host ------------------------------------------------------------------

  shards:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 64
    label: shards the data is split into
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: the records are split into sixty-four shards, each
        held whole by one host and copied to others"
    range: [8, 512]

  largest_shard:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: one copy of one shard at the horizon
    note: >-
      One copy of the stored data, with its indexes and after compression, split into equal
      shards. Real shards are rarely equal, so the largest is at least this big.
    formula: stored_data * index_overhead / record_compression / shards


  smallest_disk:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: disk on the smallest host
    formula: min(disk_per_old_host, disk_per_new_host)

  shard_fit:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: largest shard against the smallest host's disk
    of: largest_shard / (smallest_disk * one_host)
    limit: 1
    headroom: disk_margin
    because: >-
      A shard has to fit on one host, and it can land on the smallest. The pool's total disk says
      nothing about that, so the smallest host sets the limit. The margin is the disk margin,
      because the host still has to take a dead host's records.

  # -- a host is lost at the busy hour ---------------------------------------------------------

  largest_host_cores:
    kind: derived
    unit: core/host
    label: cores on the largest host
    formula: max(cores_per_old_host, cores_per_new_host)

  utilisation_after_losing_largest:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation after losing the largest host
    formula: busy_cores / (pool_cores - largest_host_cores * one_host)

  failure_headroom:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: utilisation with the largest host down
    of: utilisation_after_losing_largest
    limit: 1
    headroom: queueing_margin
    because: >-
      N+1 in a mixed pool means surviving the loss of the largest host, not an average one: that
      is the most capacity one fault can take away (ch11).

  # -- what it costs over the horizon ------------------------------------------------------------
  # The old hosts' purchase is spent, and stays out. What they cost to run does not.

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    label: horizon
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "the web service model's horizon (ch02): the refresh cycle the fleet is bought
        against"

  host_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 4500, p90: 9500}}
    label: price of a new host
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Lognormal, as in the web service model's host price at its point estimate (ch15)"

  new_capex:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: capital spent on new hosts
    formula: new_hosts * host_price

  new_host_power:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: W/host
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 220, likely: 300, maximum: 420}}
    label: power per new host
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Triangular, as in the web service model's host power at its point estimate (ch16)"

  old_host_power:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: W/host
    value: 280
    label: power per old host
    note: >-
      One number: a premise of this worked example, not an estimate of any real host, so a range would be a claim nobody made.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: an older host draws nearly as much as a new one for
        half the cores"

  pue:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 1.15, likely: 1.35, maximum: 1.75}}
    label: PUE
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Triangular, as in the web service model's PUE at its point estimate (ch16)"

  hours_per_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: hour/year
    value: 8766
    label: hours in a year
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: "definition: 365.25 days of 24 hours"

  electricity_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/kWh
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 0.085, p90: 0.21}}
    label: electricity price
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Lognormal, as in the web service model's electricity price at its point estimate (ch16)"

  annual_energy_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: energy per year
    formula: (old_hosts * old_host_power + new_hosts * new_host_power) * pue * hours_per_year * electricity_price

  licence_per_core:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/core/year
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 40, p90: 160}}
    label: licence per core per year
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Lognormal, as in the web service model's licence per core (ch15). Charged on every core running,
        old or new"

  annual_licences:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: licences per year
    formula: pool_cores * licence_per_core

  support_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: 1/year
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.07, likely: 0.11, maximum: 0.18}}
    label: support rate on new hosts
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "Triangular, as in the web service model's support rate at its point estimate (ch15): a yearly share of
        the capital cost"

  old_support_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host/year
    value: 300
    label: support per old host per year
    note: >-
      One number: a premise of this worked example, not an estimate of any real host, so a range would be a claim nobody made.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "this worked example's premise: a maintenance contract on hosts whose purchase is
        long paid for. A share of a capital cost no longer counted would not describe it"

  annual_support:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: support per year
    formula: new_capex * support_rate + old_hosts * old_support_per_host

  annual_running:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: running cost per year
    formula: annual_energy_cost + annual_licences + annual_support

  total_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: cost over the horizon
    formula: new_capex + annual_running * horizon

outputs:
  - new_hosts_weighted
  - new_hosts_equal
  - new_for_requests
  - new_for_memory
  - new_for_storage
  - new_for_requests_equal
  - total_cost
  - new_capex
  - annual_running
  - queueing_headroom_weighted
  - queueing_headroom_equal
  - shard_fit
  - failure_headroom

correlations:
  - a: peak_request_rate_t0
    b: service_demand
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      As in the web service model (ch14): a busier service is usually a slower one per request, so
      the two rise together, and treating them as independent understates the tail.
files.scenarios/old_retired.yaml:
scenario: old_retired
title: The old hosts retire before the horizon
because: >-
  The worst point for a pool bought on the assumption that the old hosts stay: they have gone, and
  demand has not stopped growing. The new hosts are the ones bought for the reference case.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  old_hosts: 0
files.scenarios/reference.yaml:
scenario: reference
title: Keep the old hosts
because: >-
  Thirty of last generation's hosts stay in service to the horizon, and the new hosts are bought
  for what they cannot cover, with requests routed by capacity. Every figure the book quotes for
  this model comes from here unless it says otherwise.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides: {}
files.scenarios/replace.yaml:
scenario: replace
title: Replace the old hosts
because: >-
  The other half of keep versus replace (ch22): every old host is retired now and the fleet is all
  new, sized as the web service sizes it. Its purchase count is the web service model's own
  recommendation at the point estimates, hosts_recommended (ch10).
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  old_hosts: 0
  new_hosts: 54
